keyVerseText: The God of this people of Israel chose our fathers, and exalted the people when they dwelt as strangers in the land of Egypt, and with an high arm brought he them out of it.
rootMeaning: The Greek word παροικία (paroikía) derives from the root παροικος (pároikos), which means a foreigner or stranger residing near but not native to the place. This etymology highlights the sense of living as an alien or sojourner, emphasizing temporary residence rather than permanent ownership or belonging. Unlike the English glosses 'sojourning' or 'foreign residence,' the root conveys the nuance of being a by-dweller who maintains a distinct identity apart from the local inhabitants.
usageInScripture: Παροικία appears only twice in the New Testament and related texts, consistently conveying the idea of dwelling as a stranger or sojourning in a foreign land. The top translations include 'they dwelt as strangers' and 'sojourning,' which reflect a life lived in temporary or provisional conditions. This consistency in usage underscores the biblical theme of believers or God's people living as aliens in a world that is not their ultimate home.
theologicalSignificance: Understanding παροικία enriches our grasp of the Christian identity as one of pilgrimage and temporary residence on earth. It reminds believers that, like Israel in Egypt, Christians are called to live as strangers in this world, looking forward to their true citizenship in heaven. This concept encourages faithfulness and dependence on God as the sovereign who delivers and sustains His people. The term also highlights the tension between earthly existence and heavenly hope, shaping a worldview that values spiritual belonging over earthly permanence.
keyVerseReflection: Acts 13:17 states, 'The God of this people of Israel chose our fathers, and exalted the people when they dwelt as strangers in the land of Egypt.' The use of παροικία here emphasizes Israel’s status as temporary residents in Egypt, underscoring God’s sovereign deliverance. This word deepens the understanding of Israel's sojourning as a stage in God's redemptive plan, foreshadowing the Christian's own journey as a stranger on earth, sustained by God’s mighty hand.
